Quantum states, dynamics and measurement · 12. How a turning point supplies the missing semiclassical phase

Far from a turning point the wavelength follows the classical momentum. At the turning point that approximation becomes singular. Derive the Airy connection, quantise a smooth well, distinguish a hard wall and estimate a tunnelling exponent with a defensible error check.

Expand the action before interpreting a local wavelength

For a stationary one-dimensional state with smooth potential \(V(x)\), write \(\psi=e^{iS(x)/\hbar}\). Substitution into Schrödinger's equation gives \(S'^2-i\hbar S''=2m(E-V)=p^2(x)\). Expand \(S=S_0+(\hbar/i)S_1+\cdots\). The leading terms give \(S_0'=\pm p\) and \(S_1'=-p'/(2p)\) in an allowed region where \(p>0\). Thus travelling waves have form \(C p^{-1/2}\exp[\pm i\int^x p\,dx/\hbar]\). The amplitude factor is physically essential: for a single such branch the current to leading order is \(\pm|C|^2/m\), independent of \(x\), as required for steady flux in a real potential. A constant amplitude with variable wavenumber would predict current piling up in a stationary region.

A local condition for this expansion is \(\hbar|p'|/p^2\ll1\) together with control over higher derivatives on the wavelength scale. Away from a barrier the phase can remain accurate even if absolute amplitude normalisation must be fixed globally. Where \(E<V\), define \(\kappa=\sqrt{2m(V-E)}\) with units of momentum. The local solutions become \(\kappa^{-1/2}\exp[\pm\int\kappa\,dx/\hbar]\). A single real decaying branch carries zero probability current by itself. Stationary tunnelling flux through a finite barrier involves a complex combination satisfying both exterior matching conditions, even though the leading size of transmission can often be inferred from the decaying exponential.

Resolve the apparent divergence near a simple turning point

Let \(x_t\) satisfy \(V(x_t)=E\), with slope \(F=V'(x_t)>0\). Linearise \(V-E\simeq F(x-x_t)\). The local Schrödinger equation becomes \(\psi''=(2mF/\hbar^2)(x-x_t)\psi\). Introduce length \(\ell=(\hbar^2/(2mF))^{1/3}\) and \(\xi=(x-x_t)/\ell\), leaving \(d^2\psi/d\xi^2=\xi\psi\). Its two independent solutions are \(\operatorname{Ai}\) and \(\operatorname{Bi}\). On the positive side \(\operatorname{Ai}(\xi)\) decays, whereas \(\operatorname{Bi}(\xi)\) grows. A bound state extending into a semi-infinite forbidden region selects the former. At \(\xi=0\) the Airy function is finite; the apparent divergence \(p^{-1/2}\) came from extending the outer approximation beyond its range.

The asymptotic forms for \(s>0\) large are

\[\operatorname{Ai}(s)\sim\frac{e^{-2s^{3/2}/3}}{2\sqrt\pi\,s^{1/4}},\]
\[\operatorname{Ai}(-s)\sim\frac{\sin(2s^{3/2}/3+\pi/4)}{\sqrt\pi\,s^{1/4}} .\]

For a linear slope, \(2s^{3/2}/3\) equals \(|\int_{x_t}^x p\,dx|/\hbar\) on the allowed side or \(\int_{x_t}^x\kappa\,dx/\hbar\) on the forbidden side. Matching in an interval where \(|x-x_t|\gg\ell\) but the potential remains effectively linear gives the connection from a decaying tail of coefficient \(C\) to \(2C\,p^{-1/2}\sin[\hbar^{-1}\int_x^{x_t}p\,dx+\pi/4]\). The coefficient two and phase \(\pi/4\) both come from the same local solution. A turning point with zero slope, a sharp step or two turning points closer than their Airy lengths requires a different local treatment.

Join two decaying tails to a standing wave

For a smooth well with two well-separated simple turning points \(x_1,x_2\), the left tail matches to \(\sin[\hbar^{-1}\int_{x_1}^xp\,dx+\pi/4]\). The right tail matches to \(\sin[\hbar^{-1}\int_x^{x_2}p\,dx+\pi/4]\). Their zeros and logarithmic derivatives must coincide throughout the overlap, up to an overall sign. The sum of the two phase arguments is the full one-way action divided by \(\hbar\) plus \(\pi/2\), which must be an integer multiple of \(\pi\). Taking \(n\ge0\) gives

\[\int_{x_1}^{x_2}p(x,E_n)\,dx=\pi\hbar(n+1/2).\]

For a harmonic oscillator the turning point magnitude is \(a=\sqrt{2E/(m\omega^2)}\) and \(p=m\omega\sqrt{a^2-x^2}\). The action is the area of a semicircle times \(m\omega\), equal to \(\pi E/\omega\). The rule reproduces \(E_n=\hbar\omega(n+1/2)\) exactly for this special spectrum, even though its outer WKB wavefunction is still inaccurate near each turning point and globally for low quantum number. Equality of a spectral result does not imply equality of spatial densities or agreement of all observables.

Different boundaries change the phase budget. Take a hard wall at \(x=0\) and a linearly rising potential \(Fx\) for \(x>0\). The solution decaying to the right is \(\operatorname{Ai}[(x-E/F)/\ell]\). Its exact energies follow from \(\operatorname{Ai}(-E/F\ell)=0\). The wall imposes a node without an Airy phase at the left. Setting the right-matched standing wave to zero at the wall gives \(\int_0^{E/F}p\,dx=\pi\hbar(n+3/4)\). Thus \(E/(F\ell)\simeq[3\pi(n+3/4)/2]^{2/3}\). For \(n=0\) this is about 2.320 versus the first exact zero 2.338; with \(n=4\) the approximation is about 7.94. Replacing the wall by a second smooth turning point would instead introduce an erroneous half offset.

Separate a credible exponential estimate from its prefactor

For a barrier with two simple turning points \(x_a,x_b\), a large forbidden action \(I=\int_{x_a}^{x_b}\kappa\,dx/\hbar\) suppresses the transmitted flux approximately as \(T\simeq e^{-2I}\), up to prefactors and corrections that depend on geometry and matching. For a triangular forbidden region with height \(V_0-E=\Delta\) at \(x=0\) falling as \(\Delta-Fx\) to zero at \(\Delta/F\), its action is \(I=2\sqrt{2m}\Delta^{3/2}/(3\hbar F)\). A discontinuous incident-side boundary may affect the prefactor substantially. It does not justify assigning a second smooth-turning-point phase to the discontinuity. For a rectangular barrier the exact thick-barrier prefactor is \(16E(V_0-E)/V_0^2\) times the decaying exponential at equal exterior potentials. It can exceed one while total transmission remains small.

Suppose two measurements change only the forbidden width of a flat barrier from \(d\) to \(d+\Delta d\), keeping both interfaces and asymptotic energies the same. In the thick limit the ratio \(T(d+\Delta d)/T(d)\simeq e^{-2\kappa\Delta d/\hbar}\) cancels the common prefactor. If \(\kappa/\hbar=2.0\,\mathrm{nm^{-1}}\) and \(\Delta d=0.50\) nm, this ratio is \(e^{-2}=0.1353\). An offset error in barrier width that leaves this ratio unchanged can still cause a large error in absolute transmission. Near the top two turning points can merge, \(I\) becomes small, and the raw exponential lacks a unitary connection to the over-barrier reflection regime. Use a suitable uniform approximation or a direct scattering solution there.

Predict a high-energy spectrum without a closed-form wavefunction

Consider a pure quartic trap \(V(x)=\lambda x^4\) with \(\lambda>0\). Classical turning points lie at \(x=\pm a,\ a=(E/\lambda)^{1/4}\). Unlike the harmonic oscillator its period changes with energy, so its levels cannot be equally spaced. The semiclassical action can be evaluated once in dimensionless coordinates and then rescaled to any \(m,\lambda,E\):

\[A(E)=\int_{-a}^a\sqrt{2m(E-\lambda x^4)}\,dx=2\sqrt{2m}\,\lambda^{-1/4}E^{3/4} I_4,\]
\[I_4=\int_0^1\sqrt{1-y^4}\,dy .\]

With \(s=y^4\), \(I_4=\frac14B(1/4,3/2)\simeq0.8740\). Quantising \(A(E_n)=\pi\hbar(n+1/2)\) predicts \(E_n\simeq[\pi\hbar(n+1/2)\lambda^{1/4}/(2\sqrt{2m}I_4)]^{4/3}\). The dependence \(E\propto n^{4/3}\) and the dimensional factor \(\hbar^{4/3}\lambda^{1/3}m^{-2/3}\) can be checked independently from scaling the full Schrödinger equation. That dimensional argument does not supply the coefficient or the half-integer offset. The action and boundary phases supply the additional physics.

Choose units such that \(H=-d^2/dx^2+x^4\). Then \(2m=\hbar=1\) in the scaled equation, and the leading energies are \([\pi(n+1/2)/(2I_4)]^{4/3}\). For \(n=0\) this gives about 0.868, below the accurately computed ground value around 1.060. An independent variational Gaussian \(\psi=(\beta/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-\beta x^2/2}\) has energy \(\beta/2+3/(4\beta^2)\), minimised at \(\beta^3=3\) and giving 1.082. Its proximity to the true ground energy has a different status: the Gaussian energy is an upper bound by the variational principle, while leading WKB provides no universal bound for this potential. Using agreement between two approximate numbers as proof of a rigorous interval would require actual lower and upper estimates.

At larger \(n\) the period relation provides an additional prediction. Since \(A\propto E^{3/4}\), \(T_{\rm cl}=2\,dA/dE\propto E^{-1/4}\); the frequency increases at larger amplitude, and the local spacing should grow as \(E^{1/4}\). Numerically compute a handful of high levels with a direct finite-difference or spectral Hamiltonian, then plot \(E_n^{3/4}\) against \(n+1/2\). A nearly linear trend is a more sensitive diagnostic of the predicted law than comparing a single apparent power from a log plot at low \(n\). Increase domain size and basis cutoff independently. A truncation that confines high-energy tails can falsely steepen the spacing, while a coarse grid can flatten the kinetic-energy dispersion. Both errors become more visible for rapidly oscillating states.

Relate a barrier action to a coherent population oscillation

Take two identical minima separated by a smooth barrier. At energies below the barrier top but above each isolated-well ground, there are two classically allowed intervals and a central forbidden region. If the barrier is sufficiently opaque, construct approximate localised states \(|L\rangle,|R\rangle\) with equal one-well energy \(E_0\). In their span the simplest symmetric Hamiltonian is \(H=E_0 I-J(|L\rangle\langle R|+|R\rangle\langle L|)\) with \(J>0\) in a suitable phase convention. The even and odd combinations have energies \(E_0-J,E_0+J\). The tunnel splitting is \(2J\), set to leading exponential order by the overlap of amplitudes through the central forbidden interval.

A single under-barrier wavefunction amplitude carries \(e^{-I}\), \(I=\int\kappa dx/\hbar\). For an open barrier the transmission probability is proportional to \(e^{-2I}\). For a symmetric double-well splitting the relevant quantity is a coherent off-diagonal energy amplitude, so its leading exponential is \(J\propto e^{-I}\), times a prefactor involving the oscillation scales and matching in the two wells. Confusing these exponents can lead to a severe error when using a calculated spatial barrier to predict a coherent tunnel frequency. The exact prefactor depends on the potential and turning-point normalisations. A direct symmetric numerical eigenproblem giving the difference of two nearly equal energies requires enough precision to resolve an exponentially small splitting.

Prepare \(|L\rangle\) at time zero. Its evolution under the two-state Hamiltonian gives \(P_R(t)=\sin^2(Jt/\hbar)\); the first full transfer time is \(\pi\hbar/(2J)\). If the observed energy splitting expressed as ordinary frequency is \(2J/h=20\) Hz, the first transfer occurs at 25 ms. Changing only the barrier action by \(+0.70\) at fixed prefactor multiplies the splitting by \(e^{-0.70}=0.497\) and approximately doubles the transfer time. An open-barrier transmission experiment over the same change instead sees factor \(e^{-1.4}=0.247\). Both tests depend exponentially on barrier shape but interrogate different quantities.

Now add a calibrated tilt \(\epsilon=E_L-E_R\). The \(2\times2\) Hamiltonian after trace subtraction is \((\epsilon/2)\sigma_z-J\sigma_x\), and the maximum transfer falls to \(4J^2/(\epsilon^2+4J^2)\). At \(\epsilon=2J\) it is one half while the oscillation angular frequency increases from \(2J/\hbar\) to \(2\sqrt2J/\hbar\). A loss of transfer contrast need not be environmental decoherence; static tilt alone yields this combination of increased frequency and reduced amplitude. Measuring both quantities and reversing the tilt tests the two-level model. If a higher intrawell level lies within the tilt or excitation range, a single tunnelling doublet no longer spans the relevant motion and a larger basis is required.

Understand the angular correction at a radial turning point

In three dimensions the reduced radial equation on \(r>0\) has a centrifugal term \(\hbar^2l(l+1)/(2mr^2)\). Applying the flat-coordinate WKB rule directly to this equation can give incorrect phases at its singular endpoint, especially for low \(l\). A way to see the appropriate angular correction without guessing is to set \(r=r_0 e^x\), mapping the half-line to all real \(x\), and write \(u(r)=e^{x/2}w(x)\). The arbitrary reference \(r_0\) keeps the logarithm dimensionless. Since \(d/dr=r^{-1}d/dx\), differentiating twice yields

\[\frac{d^2u}{dr^2}=\frac{e^{x/2}}{r^2}\left(w''-\frac14 w\right).\]

The resulting equation for \(w\) has squared local action momentum in \(x\) proportional to \(2mr^2(E-V)-\hbar^2(l+1/2)^2\). Thus returning its action \(\int p_xdx\) to \(r\) uses \(l(l+1)\to(l+1/2)^2\) in the radial semiclassical momentum. This is the Langer correction. It does not change the exact angular eigenvalue \(L^2=\hbar^2l(l+1)\); it accounts for the coordinate transformation and endpoint behaviour of the semiclassical representation. Confusing those statements would alter the exact radial equation to repair an approximate integration rule.

An instructive check is the isotropic oscillator. For \(V=m\omega^2r^2/2\) and effective classical angular momentum \(L=(l+1/2)\hbar\), the radial action over its two roots is \(A_r=(\pi/2)(E/\omega-L)\). One can obtain this without an explicit contour integral by noting that radial motion repeats at twice the Cartesian frequency, so \(dA_r/dE=\pi/(2\omega)\). Fix the integration constant at the circular-orbit threshold \(E=\omega L\), where the two radial turning points meet and \(A_r=0\). Quantising \(A_r=\pi\hbar(n_r+1/2)\) gives \(E=\hbar\omega(2n_r+l+3/2)\), matching the exact three-dimensional oscillator spectrum. For \(l=0\) the naive uncorrected centrifugal term has no inner turning point; transferring a generic two-smooth-turning-point formula into that half-line problem without reconsidering its origin is especially unsafe.

Calculate an exponentially small transmission without subtracting nearly equal numbers

In a classically forbidden interval the local solution contains a growing and a decaying branch. In a long interval numerical transfer matrices can contain elements as large as \(e^I\), while the quantity sought is as small as \(e^{-2I}\). Straight propagation of a decaying boundary condition in the unstable direction can contaminate it with a tiny growing roundoff component which eventually dominates. A plot matching the expected slope over the first few decay lengths gives no guarantee that a final tiny flux is accurate. Numerically stable alternatives include propagating a logarithmic derivative with controlled handling of its poles, matching independently normalised left and right solutions, or composing scattering matrices for short slices while retaining decaying propagation factors.

For a square barrier the exact transmission at \(E<V_0\) in equal exterior regions is \(T=[1+V_0^2\sinh^2(\kappa d/\hbar)/(4E(V_0-E))]^{-1}\). With \(E=V_0/2\) this simplifies to \(\operatorname{sech}^2 I\). At \(I=20\) its value is approximately \(4e^{-40}=1.70\times10^{-17}\). Computing \(T=1-R\) in ordinary double precision can give exactly zero since the reflection probability rounds to one. Compute transmitted amplitude or its logarithm directly and compare \(\log T\simeq\log4-2I\). At a moderate \(I\), where both currents are accurately representable, independently verify \(R+T=1\). Moving the benchmarking point across the barrier-opacity range tests both the physical approximation and the floating-point representation of the desired observable.

Resolve a wave through a classical turning point

Vary the physical length scale in a locally linear potential. Compare the numerical Airy solution and the two semiclassical branches near and away from the turn.

Open the live experiment

Connect semiclassical action to counting states in phase space

The action quantisation rule can also be read as a statement about the number of energy levels below a chosen energy. In a one-dimensional smooth confining well the classically accessible region in \((x,p)\) has area \(\Omega(E)=\int dx\int_{-p(x)}^{p(x)}dp=2A(E)\). Roughly one stationary state fits per phase-space area \(2\pi\hbar\), with an endpoint correction from the turning-point phases. The smoothed density of states follows by differentiating \(\bar N(E)\simeq\Omega(E)/(2\pi\hbar)\), giving \(\bar\rho(E)=T_{\rm cl}/(2\pi\hbar)\). This counts levels after smoothing over individual spacing; the exact count is a staircase and its derivative a sum of delta functions. A formula for a smooth density cannot predict each state in a near-degenerate doublet without additional phase and tunnelling information.

For a particle in a two-dimensional rigid rectangular region, apply the same counting idea in four-dimensional phase space. With area \(\mathcal A=L_xL_y\), accessible momentum disk \(p_x^2+p_y^2<2mE\), the scalar smoothed count is \(\bar N(E)\simeq\mathcal A\pi(2mE)/(2\pi\hbar)^2=\mathcal A mE/(2\pi\hbar^2)\). Its derivative is a constant, unlike the \(E^{-1/2}\) free one-dimensional density and the \(\sqrt E\) three-dimensional density. This leading area law can be checked by directly counting positive integer lattice points satisfying \((n_x\pi/L_x)^2+(n_y\pi/L_y)^2<k^2\) in a Dirichlet rectangle. It works after smoothing when many modes fit in the domain and makes no assumption that the rectangular shape itself models all possible billiards.

A more sensitive check accounts for the excluded axes in that first-quadrant lattice count. For a Dirichlet rectangle subtract half of the positive-axis contributions at each boundary of the quadrant. In terms of perimeter \(\mathcal P=2(L_x+L_y)\), the resulting first two terms are \(\bar N(k)\simeq\mathcal A k^2/(4\pi)-\mathcal P k/(4\pi)+O(1)\) after appropriate smoothing, with fluctuations from discrete modes beyond this local expansion. Neumann boundaries reverse the sign of the perimeter term because modes constant along one coordinate are admitted. Area alone determines the bulk growth, whereas boundary condition affects the next correction. The finite corner term and spectral fluctuations require more care than assigning one universal integer offset to every billiard.

The distinction between smoothing and exact prediction also explains why counting every computed eigenvalue only up to an arbitrarily sharp threshold can produce apparent convergence jumps as the mesh improves. If a true eigenvalue lies near the threshold, a small numerical shift changes an integer count by one. Compare a range of cumulative counts, track nearby eigenvalue residuals and study the smoothed density with a bandwidth large enough to include several levels but small compared with the energy scale of interest. Repeating for two geometries of equal area and different perimeter tests actual geometric information beyond an overall energy scale.

Measure the boundary correction in a square cavity

A scalar mode calculation uses a square of side \(10.0\) length units and reports all Dirichlet modes with \(k<5.00\) inverse length units. Find the leading area estimate, add the perimeter correction, and compare with a direct lattice-point count.

Derive and check the result

The area contribution is \(100(25)/(4\pi)=198.94\); the perimeter subtraction is \(40(5)/(4\pi)=15.92\), giving a smoothed estimate \(183.03\) before corner and oscillatory terms. The exact count uses positive integers \(n_x,n_y\) satisfying \(n_x^2+n_y^2<(50/\pi)^2\simeq253.30\). For each \(n_x=1,\ldots,15\), count \(n_y\le\lfloor\sqrt{253.30-n_x^2}\rfloor\) and sum. The values are \(15,15,15,15,15,14,14,13,13,12,11,10,9,7,5\), giving 183. Agreement at this threshold is close, while the leading area term alone is about sixteen high. Nearby thresholds can have different residual fluctuations, so the close integer agreement at this one wave number should not be treated as an exact two-term counting rule. The same calculation on a different aspect ratio at fixed area would change both the perimeter and the lattice pattern.

Measure a reflection phase separately from the travel action

In a one-dimensional cavity a quantisation condition can be written as a round-trip phase budget. Let an allowed region accumulate one-way phase \(\theta(E)\) and let reflections at its left and right bounding regions have phase shifts \(\phi_L(E),\phi_R(E)\) for unit-modulus reflection. A self-reproducing wave requires \(2\theta(E)+\phi_L(E)+\phi_R(E)=2\pi n\), with an integer depending on the chosen phase origin. A rigid Dirichlet wall reflects with amplitude \(-1\); a smooth decaying turning point contributes a different reflection phase that the Airy matching fixed. Adding \(2\pi\) to one reflection phase simply relabels the integer, but an energy-dependent boundary phase alters the spacing and cannot be removed by a constant relabelling.

A useful boundary that can be solved without approximation is a finite step \(V=0\) for \(x<0,\ V=V_0>E\) for \(x>0\). With incident wave \(e^{ikx}\), reflected amplitude \(r e^{-ikx}\) and exterior evanescent \(t e^{-\kappa x}\), where \(k,\kappa\) here are inverse lengths, continuity of the value and derivative gives \(1+r=t,\ ik(1-r)=-\kappa t\). Solving yields \(r=(k-i\kappa)/(k+i\kappa)\). Its magnitude is one and its phase can be written \(-2\arctan(\kappa/k)\). As \(V_0\) tends to infinity with \(E\) fixed, the phase tends to \(-\pi\), giving the rigid-wall limit. Just below the step threshold it approaches zero. Two mirrors with equally complete reflection can therefore produce different cavity eigenfrequencies.

Near the rigid-wall limit expand \(r\simeq-e^{2ik/\kappa}\). To leading order the exterior behaves like a rigid reflecting plane displaced a penetration length \(1/\kappa\) beyond the interface. For a deep symmetric finite well of width \(L\), the phase condition approximately replaces \(L\) by \(L+2/\kappa(E)\). This shift lowers levels relative to a rigid well of the same geometric width. It is only an approximation because penetration depends on energy. Matching logarithmic derivatives independently on the two sides is preferable near threshold or when the barrier shape varies over the penetration length.

Infer a boundary penetration from a measured free spectral interval

A long one-dimensional cavity with identical deep finite barriers has a measured low-mode wavenumber interval 2% smaller than \(\pi/L\). Under the constant penetration approximation infer \(1/\kappa\) relative to \(L\) and identify a check on the approximation.

Derive and check the result

Set \(\pi/(L+2/\kappa)=0.98\pi/L\). Then \(2/\kappa L=1/0.98-1=0.0204\), or a penetration distance \(1/\kappa=0.0102L\) at each wall. For \(L=100\) nm this is about 1.02 nm. Measure several successive intervals to see whether one penetration length describes them. An increasing penetration with energy changes the reflection-phase derivative and therefore the spacing; the physical group delay then contains travel time in the allowed region plus boundary delay. A geometrically longer rigid cavity would produce a similar single interval but a different energy dependence, so an isolated observation does not uniquely identify the cause.

Tutorial · determine what a semiclassical estimate can certify

Recover the period and level spacing from an action curve

For \(A(E)=\int_{x_1}^{x_2}p\,dx\) in a smooth bound well, derive \(dA/dE\) and infer the local energy spacing. Apply it to a 100 kHz oscillator and express spacing in both joules and electronvolts.

Work through the solution

The endpoint derivative terms vanish because \(p=0\) at both ends. Inside, \(\partial p/\partial E=m/p=1/v\), so \(dA/dE\) equals the classical one-way travel time \(T_{\rm cl}/2\). From the quantisation rule increasing \(n\) by one gives local spacing \(\Delta E\simeq2\pi\hbar/T_{\rm cl}=hf_{\rm cl}\). At 100 kHz this is \(6.626\times10^{-29}\) J or \(4.136\times10^{-10}\) eV. In an anharmonic potential the classical period generally depends on energy; use the local slope or integrate between adjacent solutions rather than assuming a universal ladder spacing.

Check whether the Airy overlap interval exists

For a model atom with mass \(1.44\times10^{-25}\) kg let \(F=1.0\times10^{-21}\) N at the turning point. Find the Airy length. If \(|V''|=1.0\times10^{-16}\,\mathrm{N/m}\), estimate the relative quadratic correction at \(5\ell\).

Work through the solution

The length is \((\hbar^2/2mF)^{1/3}\simeq3.38\times10^{-8}\) m. The ratio of quadratic potential term to linear term at \(5\ell\) is \(|V''|5\ell/(2F)\simeq0.00845\). Thus several Airy lengths can fit in a region with small curvature correction for these numbers. The parameter \(|x-x_t|/\ell=5\) should still be checked against the desired asymptotic precision; the result supports an overlap interval but does not guarantee a prescribed decimal accuracy. Bringing a second turning point within a few such lengths changes the matching problem qualitatively.

Compare a triangular action with a rectangular shortcut

A linearly falling barrier has initial forbidden wavenumber \(\kappa_0/\hbar=3.0\,\mathrm{nm^{-1}}\) and width \(d=2.0\) nm. Compare its exponential estimate with that of a rectangle using initial height throughout. What would a rectangle at the average potential height predict?

Work through the solution

For the triangle, \(\kappa(x)=\kappa_0\sqrt{1-x/d}\), so \(I=(2/3)(\kappa_0/\hbar)d=4.0\), giving \(e^{-8}=3.35\times10^{-4}\). The initial-height rectangle gives \(I=6\) or \(e^{-12}=6.14\times10^{-6}\). Averaging the potential height first gives wavenumber \(\kappa_0/\sqrt2\), \(I=4.24\) and \(e^{-8.49}\simeq2.06\times10^{-4}\). The action averages the square root of the local energy gap, not the gap itself. Agreement in mean barrier height is insufficient for predicting an exponential observable. Exact matching or a direct numerical probability current would be needed to determine the prefactor.

Computational quantum experiments

Follow a quantum state from its preparation to observable frequencies, correlations and counting statistics. Test how basis size, finite sampling and detector settings change each inference.

  1. Measure tunnelling from a four-site spectrum

    Four localised orbitals form a minimal double well. Raise the inner two site energies and ask why two states concentrated in the outer wells still acquire different energies. Measure the splitting in the spectrum, predict an oscillation in time and reproduce the levels independently with OneSimulation.

  2. Which part of a Bell correlation survives imperfect state preparation?

    A source emits two spin-half systems in the singlet state. Two observers select measurement directions separately and record outcomes \(+1\) or \(-1\). Construct a Bell–CHSH statistic from four measurable correlations and determine how state preparation, angular alignment and finite sample size affect the prediction.

  3. Recover a transition frequency from two separated pulses

    A two-level system is driven by two short pulses with a free evolution interval between them. Determine why a population measurement carries phase information. Use a scan at several delays to separate a constant detuning, intrinsic coherence loss and trial-to-trial frequency variation.

  4. When three perfectly legal spin measurements imply an impossible state

    Prepare nominally identical spin-half systems and measure along three orthogonal axes, using a different subensemble for each axis. Reconstruct a density matrix, diagnose an unphysical linear estimate and see why the choice of estimator matters in finite data.

  5. Read wave-packet overlap from a coincidence dip

    Send one photon into each of two input ports of a balanced lossless beam splitter. Two alternatives lead to one click at each output. Derive the coincidence probability when their wave packets overlap only partially, then determine how a timing scan separates pulse duration from distinguishability in another degree of freedom.

Computational quantum experiments · 1. Measure tunnelling from a four-site spectrum

Four localised orbitals form a minimal double well. Raise the inner two site energies and ask why two states concentrated in the outer wells still acquire different energies. Measure the splitting in the spectrum, predict an oscillation in time and reproduce the levels independently with OneSimulation.

Construct an operator before drawing an energy diagram

Label the sites \(1,2,3,4\) in order. The end orbitals have on-site energy zero, the middle two have energy \(V>0\) and every neighbouring pair has real hopping matrix element \(-t\) with \(t>0\). The four occupation states form an orthonormal basis for one particle. Equal diagonal energies of the ends do not make their symmetric and antisymmetric combinations degenerate when there is a virtual path through the interior. There are no direct links between sites one and three or one and four. Keeping track of every allowed step will fix the power of \(t\) in the final answer.

\[H=\begin{pmatrix}0&-t&0&0\\-t&V&-t&0\\0&-t&V&-t\\0&0&-t&0\end{pmatrix}.\]

Reflection maps \(1\leftrightarrow4\) and \(2\leftrightarrow3\), and commutes with \(H\). In each parity sector use the normalised outer and inner basis vectors \((|1\rangle\pm|4\rangle)/\sqrt2\) and \((|2\rangle\pm|3\rangle)/\sqrt2\). The diagonal outer element vanishes in both sectors; the hopping inside the middle pair shifts its even and odd energies to \(D_e=V-t\) and \(D_o=V+t\). The outer–inner matrix element remains \(-t\). This reduces the four-dimensional problem to two symmetric two-by-two matrices without neglecting any state.

Eliminate the barrier amplitudes and estimate the splitting

In a sector with interior energy \(D\), the secular equation is \(E(E-D)=t^2\). The lower root is \(E_-(D)=[D-\sqrt{D^2+4t^2}]/2\), or the numerically better \(-2t^2/(D+\sqrt{D^2+4t^2})\). For \(D\gg t\) the shift is approximately \(-t^2/D\). It is more negative for the even state because \(D_e<D_o\). Subtract the two shifts before approximating their difference.

\[\Delta E=E_-(D_o)-E_-(D_e)\simeq t^2\left(\frac{1}{V-t}-\frac{1}{V+t}\right)\simeq\frac{2t^3}{V^2}.\]

A single outward excursion produces an order-\(t^2/V\) shift in both end states. Only a three-hop path connects the different ends, so their splitting is smaller. Measuring an overall displacement of two spectral lines and measuring the distance between them test different physical mechanisms.

Predict a time trace and define what is measured

Denote the two low-energy eigenstates by \(|e\rangle,|o\rangle\). Prepare \((|e\rangle+|o\rangle)/\sqrt2\). In the corresponding opposite superposition \((|e\rangle-|o\rangle)/\sqrt2\), the occupation at time \(\tau\) equals \(\sin^2(\Delta E\,\tau/2\hbar)\). Its first maximum is at \(\pi\hbar/\Delta E\). These superpositions include interior weight, especially at low barrier. A detector on site four alone measures a different projector. Preparing bare site one excites both high and low doublets and can generate additional fast oscillations.

For \(V/t=4\), the two lower eigenvalues in units of \(t\) are \((3-\sqrt{13})/2\) and \((5-\sqrt{29})/2\), about −0.30278 and −0.19258. Their separation is about \(0.11019t\). The high-barrier approximation gives \(0.125t\). With \(t=1\,\mathrm{meV}\), \(\hbar=0.65821\,\mathrm{meV\,ps}\) and the first complete transfer in the dressed basis takes about 18.8 ps. If a measurement integrates over many such oscillations, it may return one half despite perfectly coherent evolution.

Compare spectra from three independent constructions

Use the parameter controls to vary the middle barrier and hopping. The plot shows the exact splitting and its leading virtual-hopping prediction over a range of \(V/t\). The printed result gives an actual transfer time. The downloadable OneSimulation model builds the original four-site Hamiltonian and solves its eigenvalue problem by contour integration. Compare all four eigenvalues with the two parity blocks before interpreting their small difference. A wrong sign on one edge of this open chain can be removed by a local change of basis and may leave its spectrum unchanged, so also check any phase-sensitive observable used for preparation.

Keep the hopping fixed at 1 meV and compare two barriers. Start with a 4 meV barrier and raise it to 8 meV. Record both splittings and estimate the change in the first transfer time before reading off the prediction.

Open the live experiment

Tutorial

Hold \(V\) fixed and halve \(t\) in the high-barrier limit. How do the common shift, splitting and transfer time change?

Work through the solution

The leading common shift scales as \(t^2/V\) and falls by four. The splitting scales as \(t^3/V^2\) and falls by eight. The transfer time grows eightfold. Halving both \(V\) and \(t\) instead keeps their ratio fixed and halves every eigenvalue.

Explain why a small static asymmetry between the end wells can suppress almost complete transfer while increasing their measured frequency splitting.

Work through the solution

In a two-state reduction, detuning \(\delta\) and coupling \(J\) give separation \(\sqrt{\delta^2+4J^2}\). Starting in one localised state, the maximum transfer probability is \(4J^2/(\delta^2+4J^2)\). Both the frequency and the contrast are needed to infer the coupling.

How could one check that a contour solver has found both members of a closely spaced doublet rather than printing one twice?

Work through the solution

Check the rank of the independent projected vectors and the residual norm for each vector. Then exploit reflection parity or solve in each symmetry sector independently. Repeating a low residual for two nearly parallel vectors does not establish a two-dimensional eigenspace.

The continuous barrier calculation provides a different model in which barrier width eventually produces an exponential dependence.

Computational quantum experiments · 2. Which part of a Bell correlation survives imperfect state preparation?

A source emits two spin-half systems in the singlet state. Two observers select measurement directions separately and record outcomes \(+1\) or \(-1\). Construct a Bell–CHSH statistic from four measurable correlations and determine how state preparation, angular alignment and finite sample size affect the prediction.

Relate a counted coincidence to an operator

Denote unit measurement directions by \(\mathbf a,\mathbf b\). Outcome projectors are \((1+s\,\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\mathbf a)/2\) and \((1+t\,\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\mathbf b)/2\), for \(s,t=\pm1\). The singlet has zero individual spin expectation and tensor \(\langle\sigma_i\otimes\sigma_j\rangle=-\delta_{ij}\). The diagonal entries follow because measurements along any common axis are exactly opposite and the state is rotationally invariant. Its joint probability is

\[p(s,t|\mathbf a,\mathbf b)=\tfrac14(1-st\,\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b),\]
\[E(\mathbf a,\mathbf b)=-\mathbf a\cdot\mathbf b.\]

Summing over either outcome leaves one half for the other observer, independent of the remote angle. Covariance can change while the individual counting rates remain constant. At an angle of 60 degrees the probabilities of the two equal-outcome combinations sum to one quarter, and of opposite outcomes to three quarters. Their signed difference gives −0.5. The lab models spin-axis angles; linear polarisation analysers give a doubled angle in their effective two-state representation.

Derive a bound and choose a set of directions

If a trial had four predetermined local binary responses \(A,A',B,B'\), its combination \(AB+AB'+A'B-A'B'=A(B+B')+A'(B-B')\) would have magnitude two, since exactly one of the parentheses vanishes. Averaging over a common distribution of such assignments preserves the bound. The quantum prediction combines expectation values measured on different subensembles with independently chosen setting pairs. Use coplanar angles \(a=0,\ a'=\pi/2,\ b=\theta,\ b'=-\theta\).

\[S=E(a,b)+E(a,b')+E(a',b)-E(a',b')=-2(\cos\theta+\sin\theta).\]

At \(\theta=45^\circ\) its magnitude is \(2\sqrt2\). The derivative vanishes there, making small symmetric angular errors second order. If a fraction \(1-v\) of pairs is completely unpolarised, the density operator is \(v|\Psi^-\rangle\langle\Psi^-|+(1-v)I/4\). Every correlator gains a factor \(v\). The best attainable magnitude exceeds two only when \(v>1/\sqrt2\). This is a statement about this measurement family and this noise model. A pair source and a scalar contrast alone do not define an experimental protocol.

Assess one set of finite counts

At \(v=0.80\), \(\theta=45^\circ\) the expected magnitude is about 2.263. Each trial product is a binary variable with variance \(1-E^2\). For \(N\) independent pairs per setting, the sample correlation variance is \((1-E^2)/N\). Assuming independent subensembles, variance of the signed sum is the sum of the four variances. Here every squared correlation is 0.32. With 1000 trials per setting the approximate standard error of the statistic is \(\sqrt{4(1-0.32)/1000}=0.0522\). The excess 0.263 is roughly five standard errors under this idealised independent-trial model. It is not a substitute for a finite-sample hypothesis test that accounts for an actual protocol's setting choices, losses, timing and possible memory.

Change settings and preparation independently

Inspect the predicted absolute statistic and the local assignment bound. Find the angles for which the chosen source can exceed two. Then vary visibility at a fixed angle. Small individual spin polarisation drifts could alter the marginal counts; unequal channel efficiencies could change a coincidence-selected sample. Monitoring all four joint count tables and both single-observer marginal distributions allows more checks than retaining only their final sum.

Open the live experiment

Tutorial

At visibility 0.70, can increasing the number of trials eventually make the expected maximum exceed two?

Work through the solution

No. The largest mean value is \(2\sqrt2(0.70)=1.980\). More trials narrow the sampling distribution around that value. Changing the preparation or measurement family addresses a different question.

What is the predicted fractional loss at an angle \(\delta\) away from the optimum, and how large is it at five degrees?

Work through the solution

Write \(\cos\theta+\sin\theta=\sqrt2\cos(\theta-\pi/4)\). The fractional loss is \(1-\cos\delta\), about \(0.00381\) at five degrees. Asymmetric offsets on different analyser axes need not enter the same way.

A paper gives one large value of \(|S|\) but discards all pairs for which one detector was silent. Can the ideal bound derived above automatically be applied to these retained counts?

Work through the solution

The derivation averaged all setting pairs over a common underlying ensemble. Setting- or state-dependent retention can alter those ensembles. One needs the trial definition, data handling and efficiency assumptions to interpret the reported statistic.

For state preparation and independent measurement on tensor factors, revisit the composite-state chapter.

Computational quantum experiments · 3. Recover a transition frequency from two separated pulses

A two-level system is driven by two short pulses with a free evolution interval between them. Determine why a population measurement carries phase information. Use a scan at several delays to separate a constant detuning, intrinsic coherence loss and trial-to-trial frequency variation.

Follow the amplitudes through both pulses

Use basis \(|g\rangle,|e\rangle\). Let the first pulse prepare \((|g\rangle+|e\rangle)/\sqrt2\) in the frame of the applied oscillator. A detuning \(\Delta\) in radians per second accumulates a relative phase \(\Delta\tau\) in free time \(\tau\). Immediately before the second pulse each state has population one half; measuring population here cannot reveal detuning. Choose a second pulse equivalent to projecting onto \((|g\rangle+e^{-i\phi}|e\rangle)/\sqrt2\). Then one output population is

\[P(\tau,\phi)=\tfrac12[1+\cos(\Delta\tau-\phi)].\]

The sign of the phase follows our definitions of detuning and the reference pulse. Shifting the reference phase makes it possible to check that sign. A measurement using only \(\phi=0\) cannot distinguish \(\Delta\) from \(-\Delta\). Coherence is the off-diagonal density-matrix element that the second pulse converts into an observable population difference.

Derive two envelopes with different origins

A homogeneous decay time \(T_2\) multiplies the off-diagonal element by \(e^{-\tau/T_2}\). If instead the detuning of each experimental shot is constant during that shot and drawn from a Gaussian distribution of mean \(\bar\Delta\) and standard deviation \(\sigma_\Delta\), average the complex phase, not its absolute value. Completing the square in the Gaussian integral gives \(\langle e^{i\Delta\tau}\rangle=e^{i\bar\Delta\tau}e^{-\sigma_\Delta^2\tau^2/2}\). With both independent mechanisms the measured contrast is \(C(\tau)=\exp[-\tau/T_2-\sigma_\Delta^2\tau^2/2]\). One mechanism gives an initial logarithmic slope, the other adds curvature. A single low contrast measured at just one delay cannot establish which one caused it.

Infer parameters from quadratures and a frequency scan

Record the \(\phi=0,\pi/2\) outputs, then form \(X=2P_0-1=C\cos(\bar\Delta\tau)\) and \(Y=2P_{\pi/2}-1=C\sin(\bar\Delta\tau)\). Their length estimates contrast and their angle estimates accumulated phase modulo \(2\pi\). Suppose at \(0.50\,\mathrm{ms}\) the readings are 0.500 and 0.850. Then \(X=0,\ Y=0.700\), and the phase is \(\pi/2\) modulo \(2\pi\). With an independent bound \(|\bar\Delta/2\pi|<1\,\mathrm{kHz}\), the implied cyclic detuning is \(+500\,\mathrm{Hz}\). Longer delays resolve fine frequency differences at the cost of phase ambiguity and declining contrast. Use a shorter-delay record to unwrap a longer one.

At a contrast of 0.700 the relation \(-\ln(0.700)=\tau/T_2+\sigma_\Delta^2\tau^2/2\) supplies one equation for two unknowns. Several delays, with independent error bars, are needed to identify the linear and quadratic terms. At very low signal the length \(\sqrt{X^2+Y^2}\) has a positive noise bias. Fitting the two directly measured quadratures can be preferable to fitting the length.

Explore two mechanisms

The graph holds the homogeneous \(T_2\) at 2 ms. It lets you set signed cyclic detuning and shot-to-shot cyclic frequency spread. Compare both quadrature populations with the upper contrast envelope. First reverse the sign of the detuning, then increase the spread without changing the mean. Which effect interchanges peaks of one quadrature and which damps both?

Open the live experiment

Tutorial

What is the fringe spacing in a scan of cyclic detuning at fixed delay of 0.80 ms?

Work through the solution

One full phase cycle needs \(\delta f\,\tau=1\). The spacing is \(1/0.00080=1250\,\mathrm{Hz}\). The angular-frequency spacing is \(2\pi\) times larger.

A fixed delay gives \(P_0=P_{\pi/2}=0.5\). Does that show a phase of 45 degrees?

Work through the solution

Both centred quadratures are zero, so the contrast is unresolved and the angle is undefined. A phase of 45 degrees with finite contrast gives equal, nonzero centred quadratures.

Explain how a refocusing pulse halfway through the evolution helps identify quasistatic detuning noise.

Work through the solution

The pulse exchanges the phase-accumulating states, reversing phase winding for a detuning that stays constant through both halves. Random variations during the interval need not cancel. Recovering contrast in the refocused sequence supports a slowly varying contribution to the original envelope.

Compare a continuous drive in the transition chapter with the role of the second pulse here.

Computational quantum experiments · 4. When three perfectly legal spin measurements imply an impossible state

Prepare nominally identical spin-half systems and measure along three orthogonal axes, using a different subensemble for each axis. Reconstruct a density matrix, diagnose an unphysical linear estimate and see why the choice of estimator matters in finite data.

Translate detector counts into three components

Write \(\rho=(I+\mathbf r\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma)/2\). For measurement along a unit direction \(\mathbf n\), the probability of spin up is \(p_+=(1+\mathbf n\cdot\mathbf r)/2\). With axes \(x,y,z\), count \(k_j\) positive outcomes in \(N_j\) trials. Linear inversion gives \(r_j=2k_j/N_j-1\). The trace condition is already built into this parametrisation. Positivity remains a separate physical requirement. Using the Pauli product identity, \((\mathbf r\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma)^2=|\mathbf r|^2I\), the eigenvalues are \((1\pm|\mathbf r|)/2\). They form legitimate probabilities only for \(|\mathbf r|\le1\).

Each axis can report a frequency in \([0,1]\) even when the three reconstructed components have length greater than one. This need not imply a broken detector. The axes are measured on different sets of particles and can fluctuate in mutually inconsistent directions. A state that slowly drifts between the measurements, however, can produce deviations that persist as more particles are counted. Interleaving the settings can test that explanation.

Reconstruct a specific estimate

In 25 shots per axis an experiment obtains positive counts \(23,19,19\). The reconstructed components are \(0.84,0.52,0.52\), with norm about 1.1165. The smaller eigenvalue is approximately −0.058. A fourth analyser set opposite the inferred Bloch direction would therefore receive a predicted negative probability from this linear model. That prediction exposes the issue independently of any particular plotting convention.

A simple constrained estimate minimises Euclidean distance from the measured vector to the closed unit ball. If the vector lies inside, the minimiser is the measured vector. Outside, a Lagrange multiplier or elementary projection shows the minimiser is the vector divided by its length. One can now predict valid probabilities for every analyser direction. The result minimises a specified quadratic loss; it need not maximise the likelihood of the original counts.

Why a likelihood fit weights measurements differently

For independent binomial trials, the log likelihood up to constants is \(\sum_j[k_j\ln(1+r_j)+(N_j-k_j)\ln(1-r_j)]\). The positive physical state constraint couples the components. Differentiating each term gives a score \([2k_j-N_j-N_jr_j]/(1-r_j^2)\). Thus the cost of moving a component away from its unconstrained estimate depends on both its count and its location. A radial Euclidean projection ignores these different weights. Doubling only \(N_z\) while leaving its relative count unchanged preserves the inversion vector but changes the evidence for retaining its \(z\) component. A fit using likelihood can account for that evidence.

The shape of the confidence region is a further question. An unconstrained Gaussian ellipse may extend beyond physical states near the surface. A physical point estimate does not by itself specify an uncertainty interval; a measurement report should include both the estimator and the count data or a stated statistical model.

Evaluate a new measurement using the two estimates

Fix the first count at 23 of 25. Vary the positive counts on \(y,z\), then scan a test analyser in the plane through the estimated direction and an orthogonal axis. The graph plots probability versus angle from the raw vector. Radial projection preserves that direction. Predict which orientation first gives an impossible probability when the estimate moves outside the ball. A truly independent fourth measurement near that direction is more informative about the failure than a repeated plot of the three fitted counts.

Open the live experiment

Tutorial

All three directions are measured on 100 independent systems and the counts are 50, 50 and 50. Does this prove that every specimen was prepared in a mixed state?

Work through the solution

The estimate is \(I/2\) as a description of the measured ensemble. Many preparations have the same density operator, including equally likely pure states pointing along opposite directions. The counts do not identify one particular preparation history.

A data analysis repairs a negative eigenvalue by setting it to zero while retaining the original positive eigenvalue unchanged. Which density-matrix condition now fails?

Work through the solution

The trace was initially one. Removing a negative number increases that trace above one. A valid construction must enforce positivity and normalisation together. Projection onto the state ball automatically gives both for a two-level system.

Why is it incorrect to send a single qubit successively through three projective analysers and use the resulting counts in this inversion?

Work through the solution

A projective measurement changes the state entering the next analyser. The likelihood above assumes independent preparations of a common input state. Sequential data instead require the conditional measurement operations and their ordering.

Reconstruct how a partial trace produces a mixed state in the entanglement and measurement chapter.

Computational quantum experiments · 5. Read wave-packet overlap from a coincidence dip

Send one photon into each of two input ports of a balanced lossless beam splitter. Two alternatives lead to one click at each output. Derive the coincidence probability when their wave packets overlap only partially, then determine how a timing scan separates pulse duration from distinguishability in another degree of freedom.

Track the two indistinguishable alternatives

Choose input creation operators \(a^\dagger,b^\dagger\) and outputs \(c^\dagger,d^\dagger\). A possible symmetric unitary convention maps \(a^\dagger\) to \((c^\dagger+i d^\dagger)/\sqrt2\) and \(b^\dagger\) to \((i c^\dagger+d^\dagger)/\sqrt2\). For input \(a^\dagger b^\dagger|0\rangle\), expand the product. The two one-in-each-output terms have coefficients \(1/2\) and \(i^2/2=-1/2\). They cancel for otherwise identical photons. The same-port outputs remain and their squared probabilities add to one after using the \(\sqrt2\) normalisation of a two-photon mode. The photons do not interact with each other; bosonic amplitudes for indistinguishable output records interfere.

Allow the internal wave packets to differ

Let the photons carry normalised internal states \(f,g\), which may include arrival time, polarisation and spectrum. In the coincidence sector the two possible output states are proportional to \(c^\dagger_f d^\dagger_g|0\rangle\) and \(c^\dagger_g d^\dagger_f|0\rangle\). Their overlap is \(\langle f|g\rangle \langle g|f\rangle=|\langle f|g\rangle|^2\). Squaring the difference of their amplitudes gives

\[P_{\rm coinc}=\tfrac12(1-|\langle f|g\rangle|^2).\]

Orthogonal internal states give one half, the value obtained by adding alternative paths as independent probabilities. A common overall optical phase of either photon leaves the modulus unchanged. Delay matters because it changes the overlap in time, even without a locked optical phase between the two sources.

Compute a dip with a specified width convention

Take a transform-limited Gaussian amplitude proportional to \(e^{-t^2/(4\sigma^2)}\). Its detection-time probability has standard deviation \(\sigma\). Delay one photon by \(\tau\). Completing the square in the overlap integral gives amplitude overlap \(e^{-\tau^2/(8\sigma^2)}\) and squared overlap \(e^{-\tau^2/(4\sigma^2)}\). If both photons also have linear polarisations separated by \(\alpha\), multiply the squared overlap by \(\cos^2\alpha\). Thus the dip has full width at half depth \(4\sigma\sqrt{\ln2}\), independent of \(\alpha\) as long as a dip remains measurable.

For \(\sigma=80\) fs and \(\alpha=30^\circ\), the coincidence probability is 0.125 at zero delay and approaches 0.5 at long delay. The half-depth level is 0.3125 at \(|\tau|\simeq133\) fs, giving full width about 266 fs. A width measured at probability 0.25 instead would not in general represent half depth. Quote the baseline, minimum and width convention if comparing different measurements.

Decide what a coincidence counter can identify

Adjust pulse duration and relative polarisation. Study peak-to-baseline depth before using the width to infer duration. A reduced visibility might equally arise from unobserved spectral distinguishability, multi-photon contamination or uncorrelated background counts. Blocking each input arm provides an independent accidental-count estimate. The ideal probability plotted assumes exactly one photon in each input and observation of both outputs irrespective of arrival time within the accepted window. A narrow coincidence window makes detection conditioning part of the model.

Open the live experiment

Tutorial

Orthogonal linear polarisations yield no dip even at zero delay. Does a slower detector that cannot resolve polarisation automatically restore it?

Work through the solution

No. The outgoing internal states remain orthogonal. Summing over an unobserved label is equivalent to tracing it out and removes the interference term. Deliberate projection of both polarisations onto a common state is another experiment with a different success probability.

For a lossless beam splitter of intensity reflectance \(R\) and transmittance \(T=1-R\), predict the coincidence probabilities for perfectly distinguishable and identical photons.

Work through the solution

The distinguishable alternatives give \(R^2+T^2\). For identical packets the amplitudes subtract, giving \((R-T)^2\). A perfectly indistinguishable pair need not give a zero minimum at an unbalanced splitter.

What delay has squared temporal overlap one half if the individual photon intensity has 100 fs rms width?

Work through the solution

Set \(\tau^2/(4\sigma^2)=\ln2\), giving \(|\tau|=2(100)\sqrt{\ln2}=166.5\) fs. The measured full width spans both signs, about 333 fs.

Translational symmetry and diffraction

Condensed matter and band theory

Work backwards from a scattering pattern to the repeating translations and the atoms within one cell. Learn which structural information an intensity measurement loses.

From first principles

Recover a lattice spacing from phase addition

Illuminate a row of \(N\) equally spaced atoms with a coherent plane wave and observe weak elastic scattering far away. Each atom sees an incident phase and contributes an outgoing phase. Their difference depends on \(\mathbf q=\mathbf k_{\rm out}-\mathbf k_{\rm in}\). With the origin at the first atom, let \(\phi=\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf a\) be the phase difference between neighbours displaced by \(\mathbf a\). Up to an overall sign convention the total amplitude is a geometric sum:

\[A=f\sum_{j=0}^{N-1} e^{ij\phi}=f\,\frac{1-e^{iN\phi}}{1-e^{i\phi}} .\]

Here \(f\) is the amplitude from one atom. Use \(|1-e^{ix}|=2|\sin(x/2)|\) and take the squared magnitude. When \(\phi=2\pi m\), evaluate the original sum directly:

\[I\propto |f|^2\frac{\sin^2(N\phi/2)}{\sin^2(\phi/2)},\]
\[I_{\rm peak}\propto N^2|f|^2 .\]

For a three-dimensional lattice every primitive translation must meet this phase condition. The resulting peak positions identify reciprocal-lattice vectors. For several atoms in each cell the single-cell factor becomes \(\sum_s f_s e^{i\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf r_s}\). Its squared magnitude can vanish even at a permitted reciprocal vector. An absent peak can therefore reveal interference inside the cell.

Derivation and applications

Extract atomic displacement from the loss of Bragg intensity

A lattice can keep the same mean spacing while its Bragg peaks lose intensity on heating. Consider a crystal of identical atoms whose displacements about their mean positions fluctuate during the exposure. Treat scattering in the single-scattering approximation. At a reciprocal vector of magnitude \(Q\), every mean lattice position supplies the same phase. The instantaneous displacement projected along the scattering vector, \(u\), adds a phase \(Qu\). If this component is Gaussian with mean zero and variance \(s^2\), averaging the complex amplitude gives

\[\left\langle e^{iQu}\right\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi s^2}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-u^2/(2s^2)}e^{iQu}\,du=e^{-Q^2s^2/2}.\]

The last equality follows by Fourier transformation of the normalized Gaussian. The coherent peak measures the square of this average amplitude. Squaring the instantaneous phase factor first would give unity and erase the effect of phase differences between sites. With \(I_0(Q)\) the coherent intensity of the perfectly stationary array, the Debye–Waller attenuation is

\[I_{\rm Bragg}(Q)=I_0(Q)e^{-Q^2s^2}.\]

The formula describes the sharp coherent contribution. The difference between the total averaged intensity and the coherent intensity appears in diffuse scattering. Stronger attenuation at large \(Q\) follows because an identical displacement spans a larger fraction of a scattering phase cycle. For corrected integrated intensities of the same reflection at two temperatures, taken at essentially the same \(Q\), the unknown stationary intensity cancels,

\[s_2^2-s_1^2=-\frac{\ln[I_2(Q)/I_1(Q)]}{Q^2}.\]

This comparison assumes unchanged occupancies, instrument normalization and negligible changes in the mean structure. For isotropic displacement \(s^2\) is one third of the mean squared three-dimensional displacement.

Worked example

Recover a change in mean-square displacement

A reflection at \(Q=50.0\,\mathrm{nm^{-1}}\) falls from 10,000 to 8,000 corrected counts. Its projected variance increases by \(-\ln(0.800)/2500=8.93\times10^{-5}\,\mathrm{nm^2}\). If its original projected root-mean-square displacement was \(0.00600\,\mathrm{nm}\), the new value is \(\sqrt{0.00600^2+0.0000893}=0.0112\,\mathrm{nm}\). Adding the displacements directly would use the wrong measured quantity.

Second application

Test the angular dependence with another reflection

A second specimen retains 90.0 percent of its low-temperature peak intensity at \(Q=30.0\,\mathrm{nm^{-1}}\). For the same displacement direction at twice that wavevector, the attenuation exponent quadruples. The predicted retention is \(0.900^4=0.656\). A corrected retention near 0.90 for both reflections would instead suggest a common change in illuminated volume or flux that this displacement model cannot explain.

What repeats in a crystal?

A one-dimensional chain with identical atoms every \(a\) has translations \(R=na\). Replacing every other atom by a different species doubles the primitive translation, even if the nearest-neighbour separation stays fixed. The set of equivalent cell origins is the Bravais lattice; the atoms placed relative to each origin form the basis. Choosing a larger unit cell is allowed but folds distinct waves onto extra branches. Count independent degrees of freedom per unit length as a check on any cell choice.

In three dimensions write \(\mathbf R=\sum_i n_i\mathbf a_i\). Define reciprocal vectors by \(\mathbf a_i\cdot\mathbf b_j=2\pi\delta_{ij}\). Then \(\mathbf G=\sum_i h_i\mathbf b_i\) has \(e^{i\mathbf G\cdot\mathbf R}=1\) at every equivalent origin. These vectors have units of inverse length. For a rectangular lattice doubling a real-space period halves the corresponding reciprocal spacing. The first Brillouin zone consists of wavevectors closer to the reciprocal origin than to any other reciprocal point. Later we will label collective vibrations and electronic states inside this region.

Construct reciprocal space from the primitive cell

A diffraction experiment measures momentum transfer. To predict its possible values, ask which plane waves acquire the same phase at every translated lattice point. For a Bravais lattice with translations \(\mathbf R=\sum_i n_i\mathbf a_i\), the condition is \(\exp(i\mathbf G\cdot\mathbf R)=1\) for every integer choice of \(n_i\). It suffices to require \(\mathbf G\cdot\mathbf a_i=2\pi h_i\). A reciprocal basis therefore satisfies \(\mathbf a_i\cdot\mathbf b_j=2\pi\delta_{ij}\) and generates all such vectors by integer combinations. In matrix form, if \(A\) holds the primitive vectors as columns, then \(B=2\pi(A^{-1})^{\mathsf T}\). The transpose matters whenever the original axes are oblique.

For a triangular layer take \(\mathbf a_1=(a,0)\) and \(\mathbf a_2=(a/2,\sqrt3a/2)\). The constraints on \(\mathbf b_1\) first give \(b_{1x}=2\pi/a\) and then \(b_{1y}=-2\pi/(\sqrt3a)\). Similarly \(\mathbf b_2=(0,4\pi/(\sqrt3a))\). Verify that translating along \(\mathbf a_2\) leaves the phase of \(\mathbf b_1\) unchanged. Reciprocal vectors have units of inverse length.

How far can a wave vector move from the origin before an equivalent representative is nearer? The boundary shared with \(\mathbf G\) solves \(|\mathbf k|=|\mathbf k-\mathbf G|\), or \(\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf G=|\mathbf G|^2/2\). The half-planes around the origin define the first Brillouin zone. Here the six shortest reciprocal vectors give a hexagon. With \(a=0.300\,\mathrm{nm}\) the shortest \(|\mathbf G|\) is \(4\pi/(\sqrt3 a)=24.18\,\mathrm{nm^{-1}}\), putting a face midpoint \(12.09\,\mathrm{nm^{-1}}\) from the centre. The zone area is \((2\pi)^2/(\sqrt3a^2/2)=506.5\,\mathrm{nm^{-2}}\), equal to one reciprocal primitive-cell area. Doubling all lattice lengths halves the distances in the diffraction pattern and quarters its zone area. These reciprocal positions follow from translation symmetry. The measured intensities also depend on what occupies each cell.

Add amplitudes before taking intensities

An elastic plane wave scattered from positions \(na+d_j\) accumulates a phase equal to the momentum-transfer wavevector \(Q\) times position. For \(N\) identical cells the amplitude factorises:

\[A(Q)=\underbrace{\sum_j f_j(Q)e^{iQd_j}}_{F(Q)}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}e^{iQna},\qquad I(Q)\propto |A(Q)|^2 .\]

The last sum is geometric. Its magnitude is \(|\sin(NQa/2)/\sin(Qa/2)|\), with limiting value \(N\) at \(Qa=2\pi h\). Large finite crystals have narrow peaks of height proportional to \(N^2\). The separation to the adjacent first zero is \(2\pi/(Na)\); doubling coherent length halves this width. The basis factor \(F\) sets the relative integrated strengths for a given lattice. A finite instrument resolution also broadens measured peaks and should be characterised before inferring a sample size.

An extinction is evidence about the basis

Place two sites at \(d=0,a/2\), with real scattering amplitudes \(f_A=3\) and \(f_B=1\) held constant over the angular range. At \(G_h=2\pi h/a\), \(F_h=3+(-1)^h\). Even and odd orders have intensities proportional to 16 and 4 respectively, before angular or instrumental corrections. If both amplitudes become equal, the odd peaks vanish. If the two sites have identical chemistry as well as identical positions up to translation, a cell of length \(a/2\) would describe the structure more economically. Equal scattering amplitudes in a particular probe alone cannot establish chemical identity.

For incident wavelength \(\lambda\), with the total scattering angle \(2\theta\), \(|Q|=(4\pi/\lambda)\sin\theta\). At \(\lambda=0.154\) nm and spacing \(d=0.200\) nm the first Bragg peak therefore occurs at \(\theta=22.6^\circ\), or detector angle \(45.3^\circ\). A factor-of-two error in reading the detector would corrupt any inferred lattice constant.

What survives a change of origin?

Translating the entire basis by \(d_0\) multiplies \(A(Q)\) by \(e^{iQd_0}\). Intensity is unchanged, so diffraction cannot locate the absolute origin. More generally the phase of the amplitude is missing from a measurement of \(|A|^2\). Peak positions suggest candidate lattices, corrected intensities test a proposed basis and peak widths probe finite coherence or strain. These are different questions even when addressed with the same scan.

Derive the selection rules of a cubic powder pattern

A powdered crystal supplies many crystallite orientations, so a fixed detector angle can intercept every family of reciprocal planes with the appropriate spacing. For a cubic lattice with conventional cell parameter \(a\), reciprocal vectors have magnitude \(2\pi\sqrt{h^2+k^2+l^2}/a\). Bragg's condition then gives \(\sin^2\theta=\lambda^2(h^2+k^2+l^2)/(4a^2)\). The sequence of squared sines can be used to index the pattern, but only reciprocal points with nonzero structure amplitude produce peaks.

For a monatomic face-centred cubic crystal, describe the lattice with conventional cubic coordinates and basis positions \((0,0,0)\), \((0,\tfrac12,\tfrac12)\), \((\tfrac12,0,\tfrac12)\) and \((\tfrac12,\tfrac12,0)\). For identical atomic amplitude \(f\) their phase sum is

\[F_{hkl}=f[1+(-1)^{k+l}+(-1)^{h+l}+(-1)^{h+k}] .\]

If all indices are even or all are odd, every phase factor is positive and \(F=4f\). Mixed parity makes the sum zero. Thus the first allowed squared-index sums are 3 for (111), 4 for (200), 8 for (220), 11 for (311) and 12 for (222). These extinctions encode the centring translations; adding an internal basis to each lattice site can introduce additional missing peaks. Powder intensity also depends on multiplicity and on angle-dependent scattering factors, so the strongest peak need not have the smallest indices.

Infer a lattice parameter and a strain

Suppose powder peaks under wavelength 0.1540 nm occur at detector angles \(2\theta=38.48^\circ\), \(44.74^\circ\) and \(65.10^\circ\). Their squared half-angle sines are about 0.1086, 0.1448 and 0.2896. After division by the first they give \(1:1.33:2.67\), consistent with \(3:4:8\). Indexing the middle peak as (200) yields \(a=\lambda/\sin22.37^\circ=0.405\) nm. The other two peaks independently give the same value to the displayed precision, unlike an arbitrary assignment to successive integers.

Now let the (200) detector angle fall by \(0.100^\circ\) under load. Differentiating \(2d\sin\theta=\lambda\) gives \(\Delta d/d\simeq-\cot\theta\,\Delta\theta\). Here \(\Delta\theta=-0.0500^\circ=-8.73\times10^{-4}\) rad, hence \(\Delta d/d=+2.12\times10^{-3}\). That is tensile strain along the scattering vector. A single peak shift cannot establish an isotropic volume strain without further orientations. Multiple peaks can also separate a uniform scale error in wavelength from a genuine directional strain. In the unstrained limit the lattice parameter extracted independently from every correctly indexed family should agree within instrumental uncertainty.

Peak position and width respond differently to imperfections. If all sampled crystallites undergo the same fractional change of their plane spacing, their peaks shift together by the differential Bragg relation. A distribution of tensile and compressive strains can instead broaden the peak around an almost unchanged mean angle. A finite crystallite size can also broaden it, but its angular dependence across several reflection families differs from the leading strain broadening. Comparing several indexed peaks therefore gives more information than treating a wide single line as direct evidence for a particular mean lattice parameter.

Instrumental angle calibration should be checked with a reference powder so that a detector zero shift does not masquerade as a specimen strain.

Tell a finite-size minimum from a basis extinction

Eight identical cells contain sites at 0 and half a lattice period. Sum the eight cell amplitudes coherently, then multiply by the basis amplitude \(f_A+f_B e^{iQa/2}\). Here the form factors are real, positive and independent of angle.
